title: Accept Business Payments From India As a US / UK / Singapore / UAE / Australia / Canada Company
summary: Learn how US, UK, Singapore, UAE, Australian and Canadian businesses can accept INR payments from Indian customers without setting up an Indian entity.
body_markdown:
Table of Contents


Toggle


An Indian buyer lands on your pricing page. They pick a plan, enter their card details, and[get a decline](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/payment-declined-by-bank-reasons-and-fixes/) . No explanation. They try again, you will get the same result.


No customer tries the same payment twice. So if the first one fails, they close the tab.


India is one of the largest digital-buying populations on earth, with steady demand for global software, tools and services from startups, mid-market firms and enterprises alike.


Yet the checkout experience is bad enough that plenty of finance and product teams quietly label India “low-conversion” and move on. It isn’t low-conversion. The plumbing is wrong.


When we audit failing cross-border checkout flows, the culprit is almost never pricing or product-market fit. It’s a standard international processor colliding with Indian payment infrastructure it was never built for: mandatory additional authentication, issuer-side card restrictions, and no native UPI.


Payment failures are widely cited as the single biggest driver of cart abandonment in India, and[success rates](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/what-is-payment-success-rate/) on international cards at overseas checkouts can slip to the 70–80% range, which, on high-value transactions, is an expensive leak.


Here is the part most foreign teams don’t hear early enough. You do not need to spend months and tens of thousands of dollars setting up an Indian subsidiary.


Under the RBI’s Payment Aggregator – Cross Border (PA-CB) framework, a foreign company can accept business payments from India while staying fully offshore.


##


**Why Is Your Current Global Payment Gateway Failing in India?**


Standard international gateways were designed around card rails and fraud models from other markets. India runs on different rules, and those rules are set by the RBI.


###


**Decoding the AFA Mandate**


India’s Additional Factor of Authentication (AFA) requirement means a digital payment generally needs a second proof of identity, and the eligible forms are;


- OTP
- PIN
- Biometric


In the US, a card number, expiry and CVV can complete a purchase. In India, that same flow hits a wall at the issuing bank for payments that don’t follow the AFA mandate.


The rule has also tightened for cross-border checkouts. Before the AFA mandate became a benchmark, a one-time card payment from an Indian card at an overseas merchant often reached the issuer with no authentication request at all, and the issuer approved or declined on its own risk model.


The RBI has now extended AFA to cross-border card-not-present transactions on India-issued cards, effective **1 October 2026** .


This means Indian issuing banks have to integrate this system into their payment workflow. But the responsibility to raise the authentication request sits with foreign merchants and their acquirers.


So if your gateway can’t trigger an OTP or[3-D Secure](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/2d-and-3d-payment-gateway-what-businesses-should-know/) challenge that renders properly on a phone, your authorisation rate depends on how issuers choose to treat unauthenticated cross-border traffic.


That is not a position you want to be in.


In addition to the AFA mandate, businesses with recurring billing products carry their own rulebook.


Saved cards must be stored as network tokens rather than raw card numbers, and recurring charges fall under the RBI’s e-mandate framework, with AFA at registration and for changes. Many global billing stacks simply weren’t built to speak this language.


###


**The Default International Block**


Many Indian debit and credit cards come with a default setting where international usage is switched off. And “international” is not a single toggle.


A cardholder may have enabled international point-of-sale use while online international payments stay disabled, since each channel is controlled separately in the banking app.


Your customer doesn’t know this. They see “Do Not Honour” or “Restricted card,” assume your site is broken, and leave.


The worst part is that you never understand the reason for the customer leaving or switching gears.


###


**The Card-not-Present Bias**


Global gateways also treat unfamiliar geographies as higher risk. An Indian card, processed through a foreign acquiring bank, appears to the issuer as an overseas charge.


Issuers in India may have reservations about such transactions. As a result, it leads to a pattern of soft declines: transactions that fail for risk reasons rather than because the customer lacks funds.


Three failure layers, then, stacked on top of each other: authentication, card settings, and issuer risk scoring. Fixing one rarely fixes the others. The structural fix is to stop forcing Indian payments through a foreign pipe.

##


**The Local Landscape: What Indian Customers Actually Expect at Checkout**


You can’t scale in India without understanding and integrating the native UPI infrastructure.


###


**UPI is the Default, not the Alternative**


[UPI (Unified Payments Interface)](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/upi-full-form-meaning-how-it-works/) is a real-time, bank-to-bank payment system run by NPCI.


A customer opens an app like Google Pay or PhonePe, confirms with a UPI PIN, and the money moves. No card number. No OTP. The money is transferred from the customer to the merchant within seconds.


**UPI Transactions clocked more than ₹31.53 lakh crore in October 2026.**
The scale at which UPI is operating is hard to miss. UPI processed a record 25.47 billion transactions worth ₹31.53 lakh crore in October 2026, up 23% in volume and 16% in value year on year. RBI payment-systems data put UPI at roughly 83% of India’s digital payment volume in 2024. For any buyer in that market, UPI is how payment happens.


[UPI for US businesses](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/can-us-company-accept-upi/) (and for UK, Singapore, UAE, Australian and Canadian ones) isn’t a nice-to-have, but a critical pivot point for these businesses to entertain Indian customers. If your checkout shows only Visa and Mastercard, you have already excluded a large share of Indian buyers before the first click.


However, from 15 October 2026, NPCI applied a 0.4% merchant discount rate to eligible person-to-merchant UPI payments above ₹2,000, capped at ₹300 per transaction, with certain categories at a flat ₹5.


Small merchants and lower-value payments stay exempt. How that structure appears on your own pricing depends on your provider and merchant category, so ask for it in writing before you forecast margins.


###


**UPI AutoPay and Recurring Billing**


Subscriptions work differently in India. Recurring payments run through e-mandates


- Customer registers a mandate once with proper authentication
- On a fixed date every month, the applicable charges execute against it within the rules.


[UPI AutoPay](https://www.cashfree.com/upi-autopay/) is the UPI version of that mechanism, and it is increasingly the practical choice for SaaS and subscription products where cards fail on renewal.


UPI AutoPay needs three things;


- Mandate registration
- Modification
- Cancellation


Each of these steps has separate authentication steps, so your billing logic needs to handle pre-debit notifications and failed-renewal flows differently than it does in other markets.


Eligibility depends on your merchant category and on the issuing bank, so confirm what applies to your model during onboarding.


###


**RuPay and Local Cards**


RuPay is India’s domestic card network, also launched by NPCI, with issuance in the hundreds of millions. Many global gateways don’t accept it at all. Plus, Indian customers expect Net Banking and, for larger tickets, EMI options at checkout.


So if it’s not built already, you need to build your payments page in a way that caters to every expectation of an Indian customer.


###


**The Psychology of INR Pricing**


Show an Indian buyer a price in USD, and you ask them to do mental arithmetic, guess at their bank’s conversion spread, and wonder what the final statement will say. Show the price in rupees, and the hesitation drops.


They know what leaves their account.


That’s why the ability to[collect INR payments as a US company](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/how-to-accept-payments-from-indian-customers-without-a-local-entity/) matters beyond compliance. It changes the buyer’s experience at the exact moment they decide.


You price in rupees, the customer pays in rupees, and the currency conversion happens behind the scenes, on your side of the table.


##


**How to Collect INR Payments as a US Company (Without an Indian Entity)**


Two routes exist for foreign companies to collect payments in INR;


###


**The Traditional Route**


The old playbook looks like this:


- Incorporate an Indian private limited company
- Appoint local directors
- Open an Indian bank account
- Register for GST
- Hire a chartered accountant for ongoing filings
- Apply to a domestic payment aggregator for merchant onboarding


- **Timeline** : typically three to six months.
- **Cost** : legal fees, accounting retainers, and an ongoing compliance burden for a market you may only be testing.


Finance leaders often tell us the entity itself isn’t the issue. It’s committing to permanent overhead before they know whether Indian revenue justifies it.


###


**The Modern Route: RBI PA-CB**


The RBI introduced the PA-CB framework in October 2023 and consolidated it into the Master Direction on Payment Aggregators in September 2025.


In plain terms, PA-CB lets an RBI-authorised provider onboard a foreign merchant, collect payments from Indian customers in rupees, convert them through an Authorised Dealer bank, and remit the proceeds overseas. The foreign business stays offshore.


The provider carries the regulatory plumbing.


Two features of the framework matter when you are vetting any India payment gateway for US companies:


- **Capital Requirements** : PA-CB entities must hold a minimum net worth of ₹15 crore at application, rising to ₹25 crore by the end of the third financial year after authorisation.
- **Segregation of Flows** : Inward and outward cross-border funds must sit in separate escrow accounts, and PA-CBs may buy or sell foreign currency only through authorised dealers.


One practical test. Ask any provider for its RBI Certificate of Authorisation for PA-CB inward, not a statement that it is “compliant.” The authorisation is a document, and you should see it.


This is the model Cashfree operates under, and it is the reason a Singapore SaaS company or a Canadian e-commerce brand can accept Indian customer payments without opening an Indian bank account or registering a local company just to collect.


##


**The Money Flow: From the Indian Customer to Your Overseas Bank**


Finance teams don’t need reassurance. They need a map. Here is where the money sits at each stage.


1. **Checkout** : The customer pays in INR using UPI, RuPay, Visa, Mastercard or Net Banking. Authentication happens in the customer’s own banking or UPI app.


1. **Inward Collection Account (InCA):** The funds land in an RBI-regulated collection account held with an Authorised Dealer Category-I bank in India.


Your money is not sitting in a general-purpose operating account. It sits in a segregated, regulated structure.


1. **FX Conversion and Purpose Codes** : The AD bank converts INR into your settlement currency. Each remittance is tied to a FEMA purpose code that describes the nature of the transaction, such as software services or goods sold online.


The FEMA tagging is what makes the payment legible to Indian regulators and to your auditors.


Cashfree does not add any FX markup on this conversion for overseas businesses, which matters because markups embedded in the rate (commonly cited at 1–4% across the industry) never appear as a separate line item.


1. **Overseas Payout** : The converted funds are remitted to your foreign bank account, with most eligible merchants settling on a T+1 business day basis, or on a customised cycle.


Each settlement comes with an e-FIRC, the electronic Foreign Inward Remittance Certificate, which serves as official proof of the inward remittance.


So the full chain reads: Customer → UPI/Card → AD Bank Inward Collection Account → FX conversion → Foreign bank account.


##


**Tax and Compliance: GST and OIDAR Without the Fog**


Skipping incorporation does not mean you won’t have to pay tax on the transactions processed.


###


**The Tax Reality**


PA-CB removes the need for a local entity to collect payments. It does not settle every question about what you owe on what you sell.


Whether Indian tax obligations apply depends on your business model, what you supply, to whom, and current Indian rules.


Cashfree’s guidance is the same: GST or other obligations may still apply, and you should consult a tax advisor.


##


**Understanding OIDAR**


OIDAR stands for Online Information and Database Access or Retrieval, the category Indian GST law uses for certain digital services supplied from outside India. Cloud software, SaaS, online content, e-learning and similar offerings can fall within it. Where it applies to a foreign supplier selling to Indian recipients, GST registration in India may be required.


This is a regulatory reality foreign entities must evaluate with qualified tax counsel. Whether a specific product is covered, whether your customers are businesses or consumers, and how the registration works are questions for a professional who knows your facts. This article can’t answer them for you, and neither can any payment provider.


##


**Why Cashfree is the Ideal Cross-Border Partner**


Cashfree is built on Indian rails, and it isn’t adapting a foreign gateway to India. Our infrastructure operates as an RBI-authorised PA-CB provider on domestic infrastructure, so UPI, RuPay, Net Banking and authenticated card flows are native, not bolted on.


The industry habit of burying fees in the exchange rate is a real cost to foreign merchants. Cashfree states that it takes no FX markup from overseas businesses on conversion, which is performed by authorised dealer banks. For a CFO, that means the rate on your statement is the rate you can verify.


Foreign entities with Cashfree are onboarded directly under the PA-CB framework with digital KYC, covering;


- Business registration
- Address proof
- Signatory ID
- Overseas bank details and a website or app URL.


Eligible merchants can go live in as little as 48 hours, subject to documentation, KYC and risk checks, and integration readiness: days, not quarters.


We provide T+1 settlement for most eligible merchants (or a customised cycle), e-FIRC with each settlement, and webhook-driven reconciliation to keep product and finance teams working from the same numbers.


##


**Conclusion**


India is too large for foreign businesses to ignore, and the compliance side doesn’t have to be a wall. The failures at your current checkout have specific causes: authentication requirements, card restrictions and issuer risk models that foreign processors weren’t designed to handle.


Each has a structural answer in UPI, local cards, INR pricing and a regulated PA-CB route.


Collect in rupees through UPI and local cards. Let a licensed provider handle collection, conversion and remittance. Plan around the ₹25 lakh per-transaction cap. Take the tax question seriously with a qualified advisor. And demand reconciliation data your finance team can actually use.
